title: Piano Sonata No. 2 in B-flat minor
hook: The sonata with the funeral march, and a finale like wind over the graves.

painting.title: A Burial at Ornans
painting.pairingNote: Villagers in black gather round an open grave, painted in the months around Chopin’s own funeral in Paris in October 1849, when his funeral march was played at the graveside.

facts: The funeral march came first, probably in 1837. Two years later, in the summer of 1839, Chopin built a whole sonata around it at Nohant, George Sand’s country house in central France. It was published in 1840.

He wrote to a friend that summer that he was writing a sonata in B-flat minor that would contain the march his friend already knew. Of the finale he added: “The left hand and the right hand gossip in unison after the March.”
It puzzled people from the start. Robert Schumann wrote that Chopin had brought together four of his maddest children under one roof, and he found the finale more like mockery than music.

The march was played at Chopin’s own graveside in Paris on 30 October 1849, in an arrangement for orchestra. Since then it has been heard at the state funerals of John F. Kennedy, Winston Churchill and Queen Elizabeth II, among many others.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a breathless storm with a hymn inside it (I), a hammering [[scherzo|scherzo]] with a gentle song in the middle (II), the funeral march (III), a whispering whirlwind (IV).

movements.heading: Grave – Doppio movimento
movements.summary: Four slow, heavy bars, like a question asked in the dark, and then the music breaks into a breathless, agitated run. A calm, broad hymn interrupts it. The movement is in [[sonata-form|sonata form]], but with a twist: when the themes return, the breathless first theme is left out, and the hymn comes back on its own.

mainIdeas.name: The Grave
mainIdeas.description: a slow, dark phrase in octaves, low on the piano.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, breathless
mainIdeas.description: short, gasping two-note figures in the right hand over pounding chords in the left.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2, the hymn
mainIdeas.description: a broad, slow-moving melody in D-flat major, played as if sung.

stops.hear: A few slow, heavy notes deep in the piano, ending on a questioning chord
Suddenly fast: the left hand pounds out chords while the right hand gasps in short, breathless pairs of notes
stops.happening: Theme 1, *Doppio movimento* (twice as fast), in B-flat minor

stops.hear: The storm stops. A calm, broad melody sings out over a gentle, rocking accompaniment
The hymn grows louder and faster, driving to a climax
The breathless gasping figure again
Darker and stormier; deep in the bass you can hear the slow phrase from the opening, under the racing figures
stops.happening: The [[development|development]]. The Grave’s phrase returns as a bass line

stops.hear: The calm hymn returns, now in a brighter key; the gasping theme never comes back
stops.happening: The [[recapitulation|recapitulation]] starts with Theme 2, in B-flat major

stops.hear: Louder and faster; the music hammers home in the major

notice: Listen for the opening four bars again in the stormy middle section. They are hidden in the bass, slow, under everything else.
The breathless first theme appears in the exposition but never in the recapitulation. Chopin brings back only the hymn.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Pollini takes the exposition repeat (≈ 2:25). The first editions disagree about where the repeat should start, at the slow opening or at the fast music; most pianists go back to the fast music, and the timings here assume Pollini does too.

movements.heading: Scherzo
movements.summary: A fierce, hammering [[scherzo|scherzo]]: leaping chords, repeated notes and sudden accents, played with great force. In the middle, the tempo slows for a [[trio|trio]], a simple, swaying song in a warm major key. The scherzo returns, and at the very end the gentle song comes back to close the movement quietly.

mainIdeas.name: The scherzo
mainIdeas.description: leaping chords and quick repeated notes, both hands jumping across the keyboard.

mainIdeas.name: The trio
mainIdeas.description: a simple, swaying melody in G-flat major, like a song.

stops.hear: Quick, hard, leaping chords and repeated notes, growing louder
Loud, sliding chords pile up; the music gets wilder
Slower and soft: a simple, swaying melody over a gentle accompaniment
The hammering chords return
The swaying song returns, very quietly, and the movement fades out on it
stops.happening: A last memory of the trio, ending in G-flat major

notice: Listen to the end. A loud, angry scherzo finishes softly, with the gentle song from the middle, as if the storm has simply walked away.

movements.heading: Marche funèbre. Lento
movements.summary: The most famous funeral march ever written. The left hand rocks between two heavy chords like tolling bells, and the right hand plays a slow, solemn melody. In the middle comes a long, tender song in a major key, like a [[nocturne|nocturne]], a memory of happier days. Then the march returns.

mainIdeas.name: The march
mainIdeas.description: two low chords alternating like bells, and a slow, grave melody above, in B-flat minor.

mainIdeas.name: The trio
mainIdeas.description: a long, calm, singing melody in D-flat major over a softly rocking left hand.

stops.hear: Low, heavy chords swing back and forth like bells; above them, a slow, solemn tune
stops.happening: The march, in B-flat minor, quiet at first

stops.hear: The march grows louder, rising to a great, heavy climax
The quiet bell-chords and the solemn tune again
Everything changes: a long, calm, singing melody over a gently rocking accompaniment
stops.happening: The [[trio|trio]], in D-flat major, like a nocturne

stops.hear: The bell-chords return, very soft
The climax again, louder than before

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The march sinks back and fades away

notice: Follow the left hand in the march. It never stops swinging between its two chords, and the [[sustain-pedal|sustain pedal]] lets them ring like bells.
In the trio, notice how the melody seems to float. It is a song, not a march; the bells have stopped.

movements.heading: Finale. Presto
movements.summary: Barely a minute and a half of whispering, racing notes. Both hands play the same notes, an octave apart, very quietly and very fast, with no tune and no chords. It ends with one loud blow. Anton Rubinstein, the story goes, compared it to the wind howling around gravestones.

mainIdeas.description: A single line of fast notes, doubled in both hands, soft and blurred.

stops.hear: Both hands race in a soft, whispering stream of fast notes; no melody, no chords
The opening run of notes again, as if starting over
A single sudden, loud chord

notice: Try to hear a tune. There isn’t one, and there are no chords until the very end: only the two hands, the same notes, blurring like wind.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Pollini was 42. In 1960, aged 18, he had won the International Chopin Piano Competition in Warsaw; Arthur Rubinstein, who chaired the jury, is reported to have said that the young man played better than any of the judges.

threads.title: Death
threads.body: The funeral march is the centre, but the whole sonata circles round it: the dark opening, the storm, the whisper at the end.

threads.title: Storm and song
threads.body: Every movement sets fury against calm: the gasping theme and the hymn, the hammering scherzo and its song, the march and its trio.

threads.title: Two hands as one
threads.body: The finale strips the piano down to a single line in both hands. Chopin called it the two hands gossiping in unison.

threads.title: A sonata that broke the rules
threads.body: Schumann was baffled by it. Its four movements are joined by mood more than by form.
